entry.title: NASA Moon Base: Rovers and Lunar Terrain Vehicles (October 2026 Update)

media:group.media:title: NASA Moon Base: Rovers and Lunar Terrain Vehicles (October 2026 Update)
media:group.media:description:
There's a lot of ground to cover when you're building a Moon Base.
From robotic rovers exploring the rugged lunar landscape to lunar terrain vehicles carrying Artemis astronauts across the surface, mobility will play a crucial role in establishing an enduring human presence on the Moon.
During the early phases of Moon Base development, these vehicles will help NASA investigate the lunar South Pole region, conduct scientific research, test new technologies, and gather the information that will inform future missions.
In this Moon Base update, get a closer look at some of the lunar terrain vehicles and robotic rovers helping pave the way for humanity's first lunar outpost.
Learn more about these vehicles: https://www.nasa.gov/missions/moon-base/nasa-provides-progress-update-on-moon-base-rovers/ Learn more about Moon Base: https://www.nasa.gov/moonbase/

entry.title: Planetary Defenders: This Is Not an Exercise

media:group.media:title: Planetary Defenders: This Is Not an Exercise
media:group.media:description:
When a newly discovered asteroid posed a potential risk to Earth, a global planetary defense system was put to the test like never before.
Planetary Defenders: This Is Not an Exercise tells the story of how NASA, its international partners, the astronomy community, and scientists around the world raced to observe and track the asteroid, understand its orbit into the future, calculate its impact probabilities, and eventually retire it from the risk list.
Learn more about NASA’s efforts to find, track and monitor near-Earth asteroids: https://science.nasa.gov/planetary-defense/ Download this episode: https://images.nasa.gov/details/NHQ_2026_0928_Planetary%20Defenders%20This%20Is%20Not%20an%20Exercise Watch the debut episode of "Planetary Defenders": https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jOb2DQWvDvc

entry.title: NASA Moon Base: The First Six Months

media:group.media:title: NASA Moon Base: The First Six Months
media:group.media:description:
No aim is too high. No journey is too far. No challenge is too tough.
Since NASA announced plans for a Moon Base in March 2026, work has been moving quickly to turn an ambitious vision into reality. From identifying commercial partners to sending humans around the Moon for the first time in decades, we are advancing the missions, technologies, and capabilities that will help build humanity’s first lunar outpost.
We’re going back to the Moon. This time, to stay.
Learn more about the Moon Base: https://nasa.gov/moonbase Download this video: https://images.nasa.gov/details/NASA_Moon_Base-First_Six_Months
Credit: NASA

media:group.media:title: What It Takes
media:group.media:description:
NASA is advancing nuclear power and propulsion in space to accomplish President Trump’s national space objectives.
With SR-1 Freedom, launching in 2028, we will demonstrate nuclear electric propulsion and deliver SkyFall helicopters to Mars.
In collaboration with the U.S. Department of Energy, these capabilities are key to future missions to Mars and beyond.
A new chapter of deep space exploration begins.
Credit: NASA

entry.title: Artemis III: Our Next Step Back to the Moon

media:group.media:title: Artemis III: Our Next Step Back to the Moon
media:group.media:description:
In April 2026, we flew humans to the Moon for the first time in over 50 years during the Artemis II mission. But this mission was only the beginning.
Soon after, the crew of Artemis III was announced: NASA astronauts Randy Bresnik, Andre Douglas, Frank Rubio, and ESA (European Space Agency) astronaut Luca Parmitano. Their mission will involve testing lunar lander systems in low Earth orbit.
The astronauts of Artemis II passed the baton to the Artemis III crew, as they are our next step in sending humanity back to the Moon—this time, to stay.
Under Artemis, NASA will send astronauts on increasingly difficult missions to explore more of the Moon for scientific discovery, economic benefits, and to build on our foundation for the first crewed missions to Mars.
Learn more about Artemis III: https://www.nasa.gov/mission/artemis-iii/ Download this video: https://images.nasa.gov/details/Artemis%20III%20Our%20Next%20Step%20Back%20to%20the%20Moon
Credit: NASA

entry.title: For Earth, With Love: Artemis II

media:group.media:title: For Earth, With Love: Artemis II
media:group.media:description:
Artemis II marked the first astronaut journey to the Moon in over 50 years—a 10-day test flight that carried NASA’s Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover, Christina Koch, and CSA (Canadian Space Agency) astronaut Jeremy Hansen 252,756 miles from Earth before splashing down off the coast of San Diego.
During these 10 days, we laughed, we cried, and we pushed the boundaries of what’s possible, setting the stage for future innovation and exploration—and we’re just getting started.
This endeavor tested Orion’s life support, navigation, and deep space systems and set the stage for future Artemis missions. Under Artemis, NASA will send astronauts on increasingly difficult missions to explore more of the Moon for scientific discovery, economic benefits, and to build on our foundation for the first crewed missions to Mars.
More about Artemis II: https://www.nasa.gov/artemis-ii Download this video: https://images.nasa.gov/details/Artemis%20II%20For%20All%20Humanity
Credit: NASA

entry.title: Artemis Origins: Humanity's Return to the Moon

media:group.media:title: Artemis Origins: Humanity's Return to the Moon
media:group.media:description:
In 1969, NASA landed humans on the Moon for the first time through the Apollo program. Now, we are going back—this time, to stay.
President Donald J. Trump signed Space Policy Directive 1 in 2017, setting NASA on a new path and calling for an innovative, sustainable exploration program built with commercial and international partners.
That vision became Artemis—a mission to return humanity to the Moon, unlock new scientific and economic opportunities, and prepare for the first crewed missions to Mars.
Under Artemis, astronauts will embark on increasingly challenging lunar missions, building the foundation for humanity’s next giant leap across the solar system.
Learn more about Artemis: https://www.nasa.gov/artemis/ Download this video: https://images.nasa.gov/details/Artemis%20Origins
Credit: NASA

media:group.media:description:

entry.title: NASA's Artemis II Astronauts Receive the Congressional Space Medal of Honor

media:group.media:title: NASA's Artemis II Astronauts Receive the Congressional Space Medal of Honor
media:group.media:description:
On Aug. 28 at NASA's Johnson Space Center, the four crew members of Artemis II received the Congressional Space Medal of Honor from President Donald J. Trump for their historic, record-setting mission around the Moon.
NASA astronauts Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover, Christina Koch, and CSA (Canadian Space Agency) astronaut Jeremy Hansen completed a 10-day mission around the Moon on April 10, 2026. During a historic test flight as the first astronauts to fly aboard NASA’s Orion spacecraft, these crew members were the first to travel beyond the Moon in more than 50 years and traveled farther in space than humans have ever before.
More on this event: https://www.nasa.gov/news-release/president-honors-nasas-artemis-ii-crew-with-highest-us-space-award/
Download this video: https://images.nasa.gov/details/NASA's%20Artemis%20II%20Astronauts%20Receive%20the%20Congressional%20Space%20Medal%20of%20Honor
Credit: NASA

entry.title: President Donald J. Trump Calls the International Space Station Crew

media:group.media:title: President Donald J. Trump Calls the International Space Station Crew
media:group.media:description:
On Aug. 28, 2026, President Donald J. Trump spoke with NASA astronauts Jessica Meir, Jack Hathaway, and Anil Menon as they orbited Earth aboard the International Space Station.
This is the first time that a sitting U.S. President has called the station from the Mission Control Center at NASA's Johnson Space Center.
Download this video: https://images.nasa.gov/details/NHQ_2026_0828_President%20Donald%20J.%20Trump%20Calls%20the%20International%20Space%20Station%20Crew

entry.title: NASA's Roman Space Telescope: A New Perspective on the Cosmos (Official NASA Trailer)

media:group.media:title: NASA's Roman Space Telescope: A New Perspective on the Cosmos (Official NASA Trailer)
media:group.media:description:
Our newest orbiting observatory, the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, is scheduled to lift off on Aug. 30. After launching, it will start its journey to its new home 1 million miles away from Earth.
Named after NASA’s first chief astronomer, the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope will have a deep, panoramic view of the cosmos, producing images over 100 times larger than our Hubble Space Telescope, but with the same crisp resolution. With its wide view and sophisticated host of tools, Roman will help us discover new exoplanets and untangle cosmic mysteries such as the nature of dark matter and dark energy.
Learn more about the mission: https://science.nasa.gov/mission/roman-space-telescope/
Credit: NASA

entry.title: MAX POWER at NASA's Kennedy Space Center | Nov. 7-8, 2026

media:group.media:title: MAX POWER at NASA's Kennedy Space Center | Nov. 7-8, 2026
media:group.media:description:
America’s newest and most exciting aerospace technology expo and air show is landing at NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida, Nov. 7-8.
In honor of America’s 250th anniversary, NASA and external collaborators are hosting MAX POWER, a two-day air and space festival for families, aircraft and tech enthusiasts, and NASA fans of all ages to celebrate, explore, and be inspired. MAX POWER features air shows, tech displays, and astronaut appearances from some of our most famous missions.
Learn how to join us: www.nasa.gov/maxpower
